_link.title: I can use a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve to explain the effect of a catalyst on reaction rate

toLevel2.stem: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram, what happens to the Ea line when a catalyst is added?
distractors: It shifts to the right
It disappears entirely
It moves upward

toLevel2.stem: When a catalyst is added, what happens to the shape of the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve?
distractors: It shifts to the right
It becomes taller and narrower
It becomes shorter and broader

toLevel2.stem: A catalyst increases reaction rate on a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram by:
toLevel2.answer: lowering the Ea line so more particles exceed it
distractors: shifting the curve to the right for more energy
making the curve taller to show more particles
increasing the total area under the curve

toLevel2.stem: After adding a catalyst, the area to the right of the new Ea line is:
distractors: smaller than before
the same as before
zero

toLevel2.stem: Does a catalyst change the energy distribution of particles shown on a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve?
distractors: Yes, particles gain more kinetic energy
Yes, particles lose kinetic energy
Yes, the curve shifts to the right

toLevel2.stem: A catalyst lowers the activation energy, causing the Ea line on a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve to shift to the left.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: Adding a catalyst changes the shape of the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve.
distractors: True

distractors: curve

distractors: left
smaller

distractors: kinetic

toLevel3.stem: Why does moving the Ea line to the left on a Maxwell-Boltzmann curve increase the rate of reaction?
toLevel3.answer: A greater proportion of particles now have energy exceeding the lower Ea
distractors: The particles gain more kinetic energy from the catalyst itself
The total number of particles in the system increases with a catalyst
The curve shifts to the right, giving particles more energy

toLevel3.stem: Why does the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve shape remain unchanged when a catalyst is added?
toLevel3.answer: The catalyst does not change the temperature or the energy of the particles
distractors: The catalyst absorbs energy from the particles equally across all energies
The catalyst increases the number of particles to maintain the same shape
The curve always stays the same regardless of any changes made

toLevel3.stem: How does the Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram help distinguish between the effects of a catalyst and a temperature increase?
toLevel3.answer: A catalyst moves the Ea line left; temperature changes the curve shape
distractors: Both a catalyst and temperature move the Ea line to the left
Both a catalyst and temperature change the shape of the curve
A catalyst changes the curve shape; temperature moves the Ea line

toLevel3.stem: A student says a catalyst 'gives particles more energy to react.' Using the Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram, why is this incorrect?
toLevel3.answer: The catalyst lowers the threshold, not the particle energies — the curve is unchanged
distractors: The catalyst does give particles more energy, shown by the curve shifting right
The catalyst removes energy from particles, shown by the curve shifting left
The catalyst only works by increasing the temperature of the mixture

toLevel3.stem: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram, the shaded area to the right of the Ea line represents:
toLevel3.answer: The proportion of particles with enough energy to react
distractors: The total number of particles in the system overall
The activation energy of the catalysed reaction
The amount of product formed during the reaction

toLevel3.stem: Why is it important that the area under the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve stays the same when a catalyst is added?
toLevel3.answer: It confirms the total number of particles has not changed
distractors: It proves the catalyst has been consumed during the reaction
It shows the activation energy has increased with the catalyst
It indicates the temperature has been raised by the catalyst

toLevel3.stem: A catalyst increases reaction rate by lowering the energy threshold that particles must exceed, not by giving particles more energy.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: A catalyst lowers the {{blank:1}} that particles must exceed, so a greater {{blank:2}} of particles can now react.
distractors: temperature
number
volume
mass

distractors: Ea
curve
area
peak

toLevel3.stem: The shaded area to the right of the Ea line on a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram represents particles with {{blank:1}} energy to {{blank:2}}.
distractors: insufficient

decompose

toLevel4.stem: A Maxwell-Boltzmann curve has the Ea marked at 50 kJ mol⁻¹. A catalyst reduces it to 30 kJ mol⁻¹. How should a student represent this on the diagram?
toLevel4.answer: Draw a new vertical Ea line at 30 kJ mol⁻¹ while keeping the curve unchanged
distractors: Redraw the curve shifted to the right by 20 kJ mol⁻¹
Make the curve taller to show more particles exceeding 30 kJ mol⁻¹
Remove the original Ea line and draw no new line

toLevel4.stem: A student draws a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram for a catalysed reaction. They shift the curve to the right and keep the Ea line in the same place. What error have they made?
toLevel4.answer: The curve should stay the same; only the Ea line should move to the left
distractors: The curve should shift to the left instead of to the right
Both the curve and the Ea line should move to the right together
The Ea line should move right while the curve shifts left

toLevel4.stem: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram, the uncatalysed Ea is at 60 kJ mol⁻¹ and the catalysed Ea is at 35 kJ mol⁻¹. The area between these two lines under the curve represents:
toLevel4.answer: The additional particles that can now react with the catalyst present
distractors: The particles that lost energy when the catalyst was added
The particles that cannot react under any circumstances at all
The energy absorbed by the catalyst during the reaction

toLevel4.stem: A student is asked to shade the area on a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram that represents particles able to react in the catalysed reaction. Where should they shade?
toLevel4.answer: The area under the curve to the right of the new (lower) Ea line
distractors: The area under the curve to the left of the new Ea line
The area between the peak and the original Ea line
The entire area under the curve from zero to infinity

toLevel4.stem: A student argues that a catalyst is equivalent to increasing temperature because both increase rate. Using a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram, how would you correct this?
toLevel4.answer: A catalyst moves the Ea line left on the same curve; temperature changes the curve shape
distractors: Both move the Ea line to the left by the same amount
Both shift the curve to the right in exactly the same way
A catalyst shifts the curve right while temperature moves Ea left

toLevel4.stem: Manganese dioxide is added to hydrogen peroxide. On a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram, what changes?
toLevel4.answer: The Ea line moves to a lower energy value; the curve stays the same
distractors: The curve shifts right because particles gain energy from MnO₂
The curve becomes taller because MnO₂ adds more particles
The Ea line moves to a higher energy value; the curve flattens

toLevel4.stem: A student compares two Maxwell-Boltzmann diagrams: one for a catalysed and one for an uncatalysed reaction at the same temperature. Which feature is identical on both?
toLevel4.answer: The shape and position of the particle distribution curve
distractors: The position of the Ea line on the kinetic energy axis
The shaded area representing particles that can react
The proportion of particles exceeding the activation energy

toLevel4.stem: When drawing the effect of a catalyst on a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram, the Ea line moves to the {{blank:1}} while the curve remains {{blank:2}}.
distractors: right
broader
centre
taller

toLevel4.stem: The area between the old and new Ea lines under the curve represents the {{blank:1}} particles that can now {{blank:2}} due to the catalyst.
distractors: fewer
collide
original
escape

toLevel4.stem: Adding MnO₂ to H₂O₂ moves the {{blank:1}} line to a lower value on the Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram, increasing the {{blank:2}} of particles that can react.
distractors: curve
energy
peak
mass

toLevel5.stem: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram, a catalyst shifts the Ea line from 80 kJ mol⁻¹ to 40 kJ mol⁻¹. The area to the right of 40 kJ mol⁻¹ is much larger than the area to the right of 80 kJ mol⁻¹. What does this large difference in area indicate?
toLevel5.answer: The catalyst dramatically increases the proportion of particles able to react
distractors: The catalyst has doubled the total number of particles in the system
The catalyst has increased the kinetic energy of every particle
The catalyst has changed the shape of the distribution curve

toLevel5.stem: A student claims: 'A catalyst shifts the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve to the right, which is why more particles can react.' Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — the curve stays the same; the Ea line moves left to include more particles
distractors: Correct — the curve shifts right, placing more particles beyond Ea
Incorrect — the curve shifts left, not right, when a catalyst is added
Correct — both the curve and Ea line shift right together

toLevel5.stem: Compare the Maxwell-Boltzmann representations for adding a catalyst versus increasing temperature. Both increase the area to the right of the effective Ea. How do the mechanisms differ?
toLevel5.answer: A catalyst moves the Ea threshold left; temperature broadens the curve so more particles are in the tail
distractors: Both move the Ea threshold to the left by different amounts
Both broaden the curve but a catalyst also adds more particles
Temperature moves Ea left while a catalyst broadens the curve

toLevel5.stem: A student argues: 'Using both a catalyst and higher temperature is redundant because they achieve the same thing.' Is this valid?
toLevel5.answer: No — they work by different mechanisms and their effects are complementary
distractors: Yes — both lower the activation energy so using both is wasteful
Yes — both shift the curve to the right so the effects cancel out
No — using both actually slows the reaction due to interference

toLevel5.stem: A Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram shows that even with a catalyst, some particles still lack sufficient energy to react. What does this mean?
toLevel5.answer: The catalyst lowers Ea but some particles still have energy below the new threshold
distractors: The catalyst is not working and should be replaced with a different one
The catalyst has raised the Ea above the original value on the diagram
All particles should exceed Ea when a catalyst is used, so the diagram is wrong

toLevel5.stem: A peer states: 'A catalyst is better than increasing temperature because it doesn't change the particle distribution.' Why might this be an advantage?
toLevel5.answer: Unchanged distribution means no unwanted side reactions from high-energy particles
distractors: Unchanged distribution means the reaction cannot proceed at all with a catalyst
Changing the distribution is always better because it increases rate more
Temperature changes are always safer than using catalysts in reactions

toLevel5.stem: On a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram, a catalyst reduces Ea from 70 to 50 kJ mol⁻¹. At a low temperature, the proportion of particles exceeding 50 kJ mol⁻¹ is still small. What additional change would most effectively increase the rate?
toLevel5.answer: Increase the temperature to shift the curve right, placing more particles beyond the catalysed Ea
distractors: Add more catalyst to further reduce the Ea below 50 kJ mol⁻¹
Decrease the temperature to narrow the curve and raise the peak
Remove the catalyst and rely on temperature alone for the rate increase

toLevel5.stem: A student draws a Maxwell-Boltzmann diagram with two different Ea lines (catalysed and uncatalysed) and two different curves (one for each). What error did they make?
toLevel5.answer: There should be only one curve — the catalyst does not change the particle distribution
distractors: There should be two curves because the catalyst changes particle energies
There should be no Ea lines because catalysts eliminate activation energy
There should be only one Ea line because catalysts do not change Ea

toLevel5.stem: A catalyst and a temperature increase both result in more particles exceeding Ea, but they achieve this by different {{blank:1}}: a catalyst lowers the {{blank:2}}, while temperature changes the particle distribution.
distractors: temperatures
curve
orientations
frequency

toLevel5.stem: An advantage of a catalyst over increasing temperature is that it does not create high-energy particles that could cause unwanted {{blank:1}} {{blank:2}}.
distractors: chain
